description: Jim Crow laws, segregated schools, denied votes and the legal battles that set up Brown v Board.
content_html:
The World African Americans Lived In

In the late 1940s and early 1950s, life for African Americans in the South was shaped by the Jim Crow laws. These laws required separate facilities for Black and white Americans in schools, hospitals, trains, restaurants, hotels and parks. The legal basis was the Supreme Court ruling in Plessy v Ferguson (1896), which declared that “separate but equal” facilities were constitutional. In practice, facilities for Black Americans were almost always inferior — fewer resources, older buildings, less-qualified staff.

In the South, most African Americans were effectively excluded from voting. Poll taxes, literacy tests and white primaries prevented registration. Violence and the threat of violence reinforced exclusion: lynching remained a real danger. ‘Sundown towns’ — communities that expelled or excluded Black residents — existed in the North as well as the South.

Key Fact

Three main devices denied African Americans the vote in the South: poll taxes (fees most could not afford), literacy tests (applied selectively and unfairly), and white primaries (barring Black participation from Democratic Party elections that were the only effective vote in the solid South).

Employment and Housing Inequality

Outside the South, African Americans faced different but overlapping discrimination. Restrictive covenants in housing deeds barred Black families from buying homes in predominantly white neighbourhoods. In 1948, the Supreme Court ruled in Shelley v Kraemer that courts could not enforce such covenants — but sellers could still refuse to sell. Redlining — the practice of banks and insurers denying services to residents of majority-Black neighbourhoods — prevented wealth accumulation. Employment discrimination kept most African Americans in low-wage or unskilled work regardless of their qualifications.

The NAACP had been pursuing racial equality through the courts since its founding in 1909. Charles Hamilton Houston, who had trained a generation of Black lawyers at Howard University Law School, developed a strategy of challenging the “separate but equal” doctrine by proving that segregated facilities were never truly equal. His student Thurgood Marshall took over the NAACP Legal Defense Fund in 1940 and refined the approach. Rather than attacking segregation head-on, Houston and Marshall first targeted graduate and professional education — an arena where the inequality of facilities was starkest and where courts might be more receptive.

In Sweatt v Painter (1950) the Supreme Court ruled that the University of Texas had to admit a Black applicant to its law school, because the separate Black law school provided was not genuinely equal. This ruling chipped away at Plessy without overturning it, but it set a critical precedent: equality was now measured by intangibles as well as physical facilities.

Road to Brown v Board of Education

Elementary and secondary schools were the most visible daily reality of segregation for most African Americans. Marshall and the NAACP consolidated several school desegregation cases from different states into one landmark challenge. The case was named after Oliver Brown, a Topeka parent whose daughter Linda had to walk past a white school to reach her segregated Black school across town. On 17 May 1954, the Supreme Court, under new Chief Justice Earl Warren, ruled unanimously in Brown v Board of Education that “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.” The Plessy doctrine was dead.

Thurgood Marshall was one of the most significant civil rights figures of the era before the mass movement. He argued 32 cases before the Supreme Court and won 29 of them. His patient, methodical legal strategy dismantled the formal architecture of segregation case by case. In 1967, President Lyndon Johnson appointed him as the first African American justice on the Supreme Court. His career shows how legal action formed the indispensable foundation for later mass protest — without Brown, the moral case that sustained the Montgomery Bus Boycott and beyond would have been far weaker.

Key Fact

On 17 May 1954, the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v Board of Education that segregated schools were “inherently unequal,” overturning the 1896 Plessy v Ferguson “separate but equal” doctrine. Thurgood Marshall led the NAACP legal team that argued the case.

Resistance to Brown and Its Limits

Brown v Board was a legal victory, but it was not self-enforcing. Southern states and localities responded with what became known as Massive Resistance. In 1956, over 100 Southern congressmen signed the “Southern Manifesto,” declaring Brown an abuse of judicial power and pledging to use every lawful means to reverse it. Virginia closed its public schools rather than desegregate them. By 1964, a decade after Brown, fewer than two per cent of Black students in the South attended desegregated schools. The ruling had established a legal principle but had not changed daily reality — it would take the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and further federal enforcement before school desegregation made meaningful progress. This gap between legal victory and lived reality became one of the defining tensions of the civil rights era.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about the position of African Americans before Brown, use concrete detail: name the specific mechanisms of disfranchisement (poll tax, literacy test, white primary), cite Plessy v Ferguson (1896) as the legal basis for segregation, and name Thurgood Marshall and the NAACP legal strategy. Examiners reward specific examples over generalised statements that “Black Americans faced discrimination.” If asked about Brown’s significance, link it to what came next — it created the legal and moral platform for the mass movement — while also noting that the South resisted implementation for years.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jim Crow laws, enforced under the Plessy v Ferguson “separate but equal” doctrine, created a system of legal racial segregation in the South; poll taxes, literacy tests and white primaries prevented most Black Americans from voting.
  • The NAACP, led by Thurgood Marshall, pursued a deliberate legal strategy of challenging segregation case by case, targeting graduate schools first before tackling elementary education in Brown v Board.
  • The Supreme Court’s unanimous ruling in Brown v Board of Education on 17 May 1954 declared segregated schools inherently unequal and overturned Plessy, providing the legal and moral foundation for the mass civil rights movement.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Jim Crow laws in the American South.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names a specific Jim Crow provision with accurate detail, e.g. literacy tests required voters to read and interpret complex legal passages, applied selectively to prevent Black Americans from registering to vote. Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to segregation. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the legal and political obstacles facing African Americans in the late 1940s and early 1950s.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) poll taxes excluded most Black voters who could not afford the fee; (2) the Plessy v Ferguson doctrine (1896) gave constitutional cover to segregation by declaring 'separate but equal' facilities legal. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the NAACP chose to challenge school segregation through the courts rather than through other methods.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple reasons with specific evidence — legal strategy built on the precedents of Sweatt v Painter and Shelley v Kraemer; mass protest was dangerous in the South; courts offered a mechanism to overturn state laws that Congress would not; Marshall's expertise lay in constitutional law. Shows how reasons interconnect. Secure: Two or more reasons with evidence. Developing: Describes the strategy without explaining the choice of method. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why voting rights were so important to African Americans in the South in the late 1940s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) without the vote, African Americans had no way to elect politicians who would change discriminatory laws at state level, leaving them permanently subject to Jim Crow; (2) voting was a symbol of full citizenship — its denial reinforced second-class status and the accompanying discrimination in education, employment and housing. Each reason includes specific evidence and explanation. Secure: Two reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: Two reasons identified without clear development. Emerging: One weak point.

practice_questions.text: How significant was Brown v Board of Education in improving the position of African Americans?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis — significant because it overturned Plessy and provided a legal basis for desegregation; gave the civil rights movement moral authority; showed the Supreme Court could be an agent of change. But limitations: implementation was resisted (Brown II 1955 allowed 'all deliberate speed'; Little Rock 1957 showed federal force was still needed); the ruling addressed schools, not voting rights or employment; mass protest and further legislation were still required. Integrated judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence. Developing: Describes Brown without weighing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the challenges facing African Americans in the USA in the years before Brown v Board of Education 1954.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering legal segregation (Jim Crow, Plessy), disfranchisement (poll tax, literacy tests, white primaries), economic disadvantage (employment, housing, redlining) and violence (lynching, sundown towns). Reaches an integrated judgement about which challenges were most significant or interconnected. Well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several challenges with evidence and some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes conditions with limited structure. Emerging: Brief narrative.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the legal basis for racial segregation in the American South, established in 1896?
Which NAACP lawyer led the legal team that argued Brown v Board of Education before the Supreme Court?
The doctrine used to justify segregated facilities was known as "separate but _____."
In 1948, the Supreme Court ruled in Shelley v Kraemer that courts could not enforce _____ covenants that prevented Black families from buying homes in white neighbourhoods.
Match each term to its definition:
right: State and local laws enforcing racial segregation in public life
A fee charged to voters that most Black Americans could not afford
A selective reading test used to exclude Black voters from registration

flashcard_questions.q: What did Plessy v Ferguson (1896) rule?
flashcard_questions.a: That 'separate but equal' facilities were constitutional, providing the legal basis for Jim Crow.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three mechanisms Southern states used to prevent Black Americans from voting.
flashcard_questions.a: Poll taxes, literacy tests and white primaries.
A Supreme Court ruling that Texas must admit a Black student to its law school because the separate provision was not genuinely equal.
A Supreme Court ruling that courts could not enforce restrictive housing covenants barring Black buyers.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Supreme Court rule in Brown v Board of Education?
What did Brown v Board rule?
flashcard_questions.a: That segregated schools were 'inherently unequal,' overturning Plessy v Ferguson.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was Chief Justice when Brown v Board was decided?
What strategy did Thurgood Marshall use before tackling school segregation?
flashcard_questions.a: He first challenged segregation in graduate and professional education, where inequality was most obvious.

flashcard_questions.q: Who trained Thurgood Marshall and developed the NAACP legal strategy?
flashcard_questions.a: Charles Hamilton Houston at Howard University Law School.
Communities that expelled or excluded Black residents, found in the North as well as the South.

glossary_terms.definition: State and local laws passed in the American South from the 1870s onwards that enforced racial segregation in public life.
A fee charged to voters in some Southern states that most Black Americans and poor whites could not afford, used to suppress African American voting.
Tests imposed on voters requiring them to read and interpret complex legal or constitutional passages, applied selectively to exclude Black voters.
Whites-only Democratic Party primary elections that excluded Black voters from the only meaningful vote in the one-party South.
The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909, which pursued racial equality through legal challenges, lobbying and public campaigns.
Organised legal and political resistance by Southern states and politicians to the enforcement of the Brown v Board desegregation ruling.
